newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile sees stronger Chinese copper demand in H2.
newsitem.headline: Chile sees stronger Chinese copper demand in H2.

text.p: Chile expects Chinese demand for copper to strengthen in the second half of the year after tepid demand in the first, the Chilean Copper Commission (Cochilco) market research head Aldo Picozzi said.

Cochilco was so far sticking to its average price estimate of $1.00 to $1.05 for the whole year but will review the estimate in early July, partly in light of expectations for heavier Chinese demand, said Picozzi.
Demand will be tempered by the seasonal fall in economic activity in North America and Europe during the summer vacation period, he said.

"The Chinese normally buy in the second half of the year," Picozzi told Reuters. But in the first half, the Chinese made "only small purchases and even a few sales and they haven't shown if they're going to start purchasing again in the second half, but we expect that to happen."
"We should see stronger purchasing activity by the Chinese in the second half," he said.

Prices so far this year have vastly surpassed Cochilco's targets of 97 cents a pound, later revised up to $1.00-$1.05 per pound, but the commission is cautious about nudging the estimate up again, he said.
"The first half has surpassed all the predictions, but looking toward the second half it's really going to depend a lot on the behavior of the Chinese," he said.

Chile expects higher Asian demand to absorb supply influx coming onto the market starting this year and lasting to about the year 2001, he said. Most studies point to a slump in prices starting in 1998 due to greater supply, mainly from Chile and Indonesia, followed by a trend toward higher prices from about 2001 after the current crop of megaprojects and expansions have come on stream, he said.

"As of 1998 the market will probably go into over-supply, after all these deficit cycles we've had over the past three years," he said. "The implications of this on markets will depend fundamentally on the demand side. Until the end of the century at least, economic activity in the developed countries looks it's going to be strong...and that copper demand will be positive."

"There is over-supply, but it's of a magnitude perfectly manageable by the market. I wouldn't expect any great imbalances in the market," he said. "That balance in the market is going to depend very heavily on the Chinese."

China's annual copper demand outstrips domestic supply by about 400,000 tonnes and Cochilco, the Chilean government's main copper study body, does not expect its local production to rise much in the coming years, said Picozzi.
"China has relatively small and quite dispersed copper resources, and for that reason there is no chance for the moment of China developing great copper projects.

"Therefore they're going to be very dependent on imports," he said. "China is going to be good market, but what's difficult to predict is the behavior of their purchases. They buy normally from traders, and there isn't a very direct relation between producer and consumer in this case."
Chinese metals officials have come to Chile over the past couple of years to scout the possibility of buying into a Chilean copper deposit, which the aim of guaranteeing a share of production.
Picozzi said the Chinese interest lay in smaller projects.
"I think the Chinese are looking for medium and smaller projects. They don't have experience in projects of a great magnitude and nor do I think they have the capital for large projects."
